title: The teacher
hookLine: a flower held up, a smile, and nothing said: Zen stresses face-to-face teaching

cards: Zen tells a story about a sermon with no words in it. The Buddha stands before a gathering of his followers, and instead of speaking, he lifts a single flower and turns it in his fingers. Nobody knows what to make of it.

Except one disciple, Mahakashyapa, who smiles. And the Buddha, the story says, declares that something has passed to him, something the words of a sermon couldn't hold. A flower, a smile, and the beginning of a lineage.

teach.b: Zen puts great weight on the teacher, and on meeting face to face. First, the flower. The story is told as a case in The Gateless Gate, the same collection that opens with Zhaozhou's mu.
Zen tells it as its own origin story, and its point is the picture: understanding passing between two people, directly. Second, the old verse.

teach.h: OUTSIDE THE SCRIPTURES, NOT IN WORDS.
teach.b: Tradition attributes to Bodhidharma, the teacher said to have carried Zen to China, a short description of the school, in paraphrase: a special transmission outside the scriptures, not depending on words and letters, pointing straight at the mind.
Third, the catch. That doesn't make Zen against books. This whole week has leaned on them: Dogen's writings, The Gateless Gate, Hakuin, Suzuki's talks.
The point is that books aren't enough.
A book can't see you. It can't tell when your answer to a koan is clever and when it's real.
That's the teacher's job, in the private meeting we met earlier this week, where a student brings a response and a teacher looks back.

teach.h: A LINE OF TEACHERS, PERSON TO PERSON.
teach.b: Fourth, the line of people. Zen schools keep lineages: chains of teachers and students, each taught by someone who was taught by someone.
Tradition says Dogen crossed the sea to China in search of a teacher; that journey is how he met the old cook.
Which leaves a plain question: who, in your own life, has taught you something face to face that no page could?

how: Zen students usually practice under a teacher, meeting in private interviews to bring questions and koan responses, and Zen schools trace their teachers in lineages.

games.q: the Buddha stands before a crowd and, without a word, holds up a flower. what does Mahakashyapa do?
games.why: he smiles, and the story says something passes to him that a sermon's words couldn't hold.

practice: Bring to mind one person who taught you something in person: a grandparent at a stove, a coach, a boss who showed you how, a friend who said the hard thing to your face.
Let their face come clear, and ask what they passed on that you couldn't have read. If you pray, hold them in your prayer; if not, just sit with them a moment, face to face in memory.

wordCard.voice: The teacher. In Zen, the person who meets you face to face, and passes on what words alone can't carry. Today's word.

orig.note: Japanese: mind to mind, a phrase Zen uses for teaching that passes directly between teacher and student.

carryVoice: Your line: face to face. Some things only pass from one person to another. That's today, done.
